text.en: The Mashgiach reads the Mishnah's unusual wording, stating the first of Shevat before naming Beis Shammai, as a sign that Beis Shammai's view is relevant even now, because it will be the halacha when Moshiach comes.
According to the Mashgiach, belief in Moshiach shows itself in practice: a farmer who truly expects him this year goes out to mark his trees on Rosh Chodesh Shevat too.
The Mashgiach reads 'the day Pharaoh was born' as the day that caused him to be born: the day he fulfilled his mission of bringing Yosef out of prison to rule Egypt.
The Mashgiach says that whatever came before a person fulfills his mission is as if non-existent, even if a birth date is registered at City Hall.
The Mashgiach ties the end of the shiur back to its beginning: the coming of Moshiach will be the Rosh Hashanah for the tree of Klal Yisrael.
The translation of the Torah into Greek, though it raised the nations above idol worship, was the Torah itself going into galus, like a Jew leaving Eretz Yisrael for gentile territory.
Just as a pure person perceives a hidden light in the Chanukah and Shabbos candles, he should perceive a hidden darkness in the gentile decorations of the season.
Whatever exists in place corresponds to something in time: Dan's place at the end of the camp corresponds to the last period of Jewish history, our generation.
The foot of the tav, which reaches outside the camp of holiness, is Dan, and the tav itself is formed of a dalet and a nun, the letters of Dan.

Yocheved was born exactly between the walls as the family entered Mitzrayim because galus cannot begin without the redeemer already prepared, just as the first day of Pesach determines the day of Tisha B'Av.
The pearl of geulah is found in the depths of darkness, so our generation, sunk lower than any before, is the one that dives down to bring up such treasures.
The initial letters of Gadlu laShem iti uneromemah shemo, the passuk of Teves, spell Shaul, the culprit among the seventy, teaching that even the fallen will be raised to join in Hashem's praise.

A beginning holds the strength of the whole: just as the first day of Sefirah already carries the fiftieth day, so Teves, opening the last degel, carries the full weight of the end, while Adar, at rock bottom, must rise.
Since everything foretold in Haazinu, all the troubles of galus, has already come true, the one missing part, the geulah, is certain, and it does not depend on teshuvah.
Using the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of space, time and soul, the Mashgiach explains that just as there are places where the Torah forbids learning, there must be a time, and that is Nittel.
The Jews of the last galus are the most precious to Hashem because their night is so dark that even a small act of avodah, like a hurried Minchah, is precious to Him.

The word 'samach' teaches that mere nearness to a rasha lets his tumah in even before any wall is breached, and the same power works for good when one is near a tzaddik, as Yehudah felt kedushah near Yosef.
The order of the letters decides which middah rules: masculine first means chesed sweetens din, feminine first means din dominates, which is why Esav put his wives before his sons.
Writing right to left follows the Aleph-Beis order of chesed: Esav writes the other way, while the descendants of Avraham also write from right to left.
Tu B'Shvat falls on the fifteenth because the din of Teves overlaps into the first half of Shevat, just as the din of Tammuz lasts in Av until Chamishah Asar B'Av.
Seraf equals 580, the numerical value of the two names of tumah and of Seir, and ilan equals 91, Havaya and Adnus together; the sap rising in the tree is tumah being raised into kedushah.
The roshei teivos of the passuk for Nissan read in the Aleph-Beis order, while the arrangement of Tammuz and Teves comes from sofei teivos, the Aleph-Beis backwards.
In the borei pri ha'etz of Tu B'Shvat lies a remez to the pri etz hadar, the esrog, and the great success of Klal Yisrael comes through the four minim.
The tree and the moon are the 'two witnesses' that the Jewish people, which seems dead to the nations, will revive, which is why the new year of the trees falls in the week of Parshas HaChodesh.
Beis Shammai, belonging to the world of Moshiach, sense renewal already at its point of origin, so their new year for trees is Rosh Chodesh Shevat, when the renewal is still only a point.
The Mishnah states Beis Shammai's view as the main one because, unlike other halachos, here a Jew awaiting Moshiach already needs to know their ruling, since it may apply retroactively.
Nature keeps the Torah of creation as a mitzvah: grass grows by the same kind of command by which a Jew wears tzitzis, so a miracle is a change in the Torah and must follow the Torah's own rules.
The world, like the human body, has a built-in control system: just as a fever fights germs, history and the Flood show that no creature can ruin nature beyond a set limit.
The nations' demand to internationalize Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim comes from sensing that it is the root of the world, so being driven from it feels like being driven off the planet.

The whole Torah from Bereishis to 'HaChodesh hazeh lachem' is an introduction to the first mitzvah and an answer to the nations why only the nation that is 'reishis' may hold the land that is 'reishis'.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah's case shows that 'beyond the letter of the law' is relative: for a person of his stature, that very standard was the law.
'Vachai bahem' is read by level: for a tzaddik whose life is bound up with Torah, being drawn away from a mitzvah is itself a loss of life.
Yovel, as the eighth after seven times seven, belongs to the same level as milah on the eighth day: something above the natural order of the seven days of creation.
The Rashbam's 'all his days' and Chazal's 'until Yovel' meet: since Yovel is above the world, 'le'olam' in its deepest sense means the world of Yovel.
The acceleration of inventions and communication in our time is like the rush of erev Shabbos before Shabbos arrives.

The threefold parallel of place, time and soul applies to impurity as well: the Mashgiach sets the beis hakisei, the one punished in boiling filth, and Nittel side by side as impurity's place, person and time.
Following the Bnei Yissaschar, the punishment of boiling filth fits wisdom cut off from holiness, which is like waste separated from the body.
The pearl is set above finer and costlier stones because it was brought from the darkness of the depths, and so the simple Jew's struggle in a dark time is placed at the head of the King's crown.
Learning amid the noise of a subway, concentrating on a Gemara or a chassidish sefer, may be prized in Heaven like the pearl, because it is brought out of a place of darkness.
Sleep does tikkunim just as eating does birurim, and it is a kind of techiyas hamesim from which a person rises a new creation.
A tzaddik reads 'ad masai atzel tishkav' as faulting the lazy man not for rising late but for lying down late.
The halachic order of blessings on the seven species, by closeness to the word Eretz, is read as a ranking of closeness to Olam Haba and yiras shamayim.

Of all the measures learned from the seven species, only the pomegranate's is negative: it defines when a vessel stops being a vessel, so it speaks of what is outside the Torah's measures, as the farthest Jews are.

The dispute of Rav Hamnuna and Rav Chisda over dates and pomegranates turns on whether 'Eretz chitah' is like 'a cup of wine', a place holding the fruit, or like 'a cup of gold', the fruit's very essence being bound to Eretz.

Heaven rejected the date parable for Acher but accepted the pomegranate parable because, by Rabbah bar Shila's reckoning, the last fruit is the pomegranate, which is still bound to Eretz and so to Olam Haba.
The Torah writes Eretz twice, though listing the fruits in order would have sufficed, to show that every fruit, and so every Jew, has a bond to Olam Haba, even the Torah of Acher.
The spies' fall is tied to the season: they went in Tammuz and Av, the pomegranate of the year, and Moshe's 'take of the fruit' was strength for a low time.

The order of the months follows the body of Adam HaRishon: Nissan is the head and Adar the heel, so Adar belongs to the souls lowest in time and in level, and Purim's miracle is the miracle of those lowest Jews.
At the very feast whose enjoyment brought Haman's decree, Hashem was already preparing the salvation by removing Vashti so that Esther could come in.
Amalek's essence is to plant doubts in emunah, and that is the cloak that hides Hashem; this is why Hashem's name and open miracles are absent from the Megillah.
HaMelech, kes Kah and Haman each equal 95 in gematria, linking the King who stands behind the Megillah to the incomplete name caused by Amalek.
Hashem's name does appear in the Megillah, but hidden at its turning points, such as the words read in one breath by a knowledgeable ba'al korei.
Parah and Pur are equal in gematria with the kolel, and Parshas Parah is a step beyond Purim: Purim comforts those left outside the camp, while Parah purifies them and brings them inside.

Parah is read just before Parshas HaChodesh so that when the Satan claims there is no reason to redeem the Jews, Hashem can answer that as they keep a chok without a reason, He can redeem them without one.
Nachash and Satan share a gematria; the ches of the Nachash, open below, inverts into the tes of the Satan, open above, and the two letters together spell chet, sin.
The Nachash could not tempt Adam and Chava with bodily desire, only with a higher intellect, and so the cure for the death he brought is a mitzvah kept without understanding.
How Parah Adumah works and when Moshiach will come are the two related matters where the mind meets a red light, since both concern the end of death in the world.

The Eitz HaDaas was a vine whose grapes Adam was meant to keep for Kiddush on Shabbos; the golden calf and Shaul's offering repeated that failure to wait, while Dovid, who waited, is the root of Moshiach.
Haman took Adar, the last month, as the end of the Jews, but for Jews time is a circle: the end touches the beginning and everything starts over.

The Egel was the same sin as the Eitz HaDaas, acting on one's own understanding, and therefore it brought back the death that Matan Torah had abolished; Parah only partly atones, removing tumas meis but not death itself.
The Satan's argument against the Geulah is that there is no reason for it, and Parah, a mitzvah with no reason that Jews keep anyway, answers him in kind.
Parah is read before both seasons of potential Geulah: before Nisan, when chesed is aroused, and as Parshas Chukas before the three weeks, when rachamim is aroused through the Churban.
In the Beis HaMikdash there was no hester panim, so even the aged Chafetz Chaim would have reached the Mizbeach first if he had the merit; the race measured merit, not strength.
Since no two Jews stand on the same level, a tie in the race was a sign that on that day merits did not count and Hashem was leading as with children, so the whole group entered the goral.
Mikveh requires one's own act of immersion and cannot remove tumas meis, while the water of Parah is sprinkled on a person by someone else, from above, and purifies even tumas meis.

The feminine 'hasheinis' refers not to the second month but to the second reading of the Megillah: in a leap year it is read first in heaven on Purim Katan, and the second reading is therefore more powerful.
The leap year is read as the moon (Klal Yisrael) falling behind the sun (Hashem); in the first Adar we are too far from Him to keep Purim properly.
The pauses in spiritual life are like the beat in music or the pause between heartbeats: they are part of life, and after the pause the fervor returns stronger.
'Hamelech', 'kes Kah' and 'Haman' all equal 95 in gematria: Haman's existence is what reduces Hashem's revealed name to the hidden 'king', and 'machi Amalek' equals 'kisei Havayah'.
A miracle that comes through perfect timing within nature is greater than one that breaks nature, and the Megillah's miracle has countless such pieces falling into place.
Purim costumes embody the lesson: just as one is not alarmed by a costumed visitor, one should see that world leaders are costumes over Hashem's hand.
Because David saw Hashem behind Shimi's curse and spared him, Mordechai, Shimi's descendant, was born to defeat Haman's philosophy of chance and to write the Megillah.
Haman's ten thousand kikar were charity, given to neutralize the merit of the Jews' half-shekels.
The only silver of the Mishkan that ended up outside the holy courtyard, the protruding hooks, came from the extra Jews beyond 600,000 whom the clouds had expelled.
The last eight pesukim of the Torah are pesukim of forgetting, and the souls outside the camp correspond to them; that is why Moshe Rabbeinu forgot their silver, while Hashem forgets no Jew.
The extra yud in 'Yehudim' that is written but not read, and the kashrus of a Megillah with half-erased letters, show that imperfect Jews still belong in the Megillah.
Haman rejoiced that the lot fell on Adar because he thought the Jewish year ends there, but the Jewish year is a circle and Nisan follows Adar, as Moshiach follows the last generation.
Tzedakah given on Purim is elevated above ordinary tzedakah, as an esrog on Sukkos calls for a different brachah than an esrog eaten on Purim.

The Mashgiach reads the Mishnah 'all of Israel has a share' as naming a world called 'Kol Yisrael', the root of the souls in Yaakov Avinu, where even those the Mishnah excludes are not rejected, because the trace of holiness in a Jew can never be erased.

The Jews 'at the end of the Sefer Torah' are like the hooks of the Mishkan's pillars that Moshe Rabbeinu forgot, which protrude outside; Amalek and Haman thought such Jews were forgotten, but the Torah ends with 'before the eyes of all Israel' and swings right back into Bereishis.

'The king loved Esther more than all the women' refers to Hashem's love for the generation of concealment, which suffered from not feeling His love and still held on to Him, more than for earlier generations of great tzaddikim.

The lottery of Purim and Yom Kippur shows a choice with no reason, like a lottery win or a bride who finds favor beyond her qualities: Hashem's bond with His people comes from a will beyond reason, so even when Yaakov looks like Esav, Hashem knows he is His.
Holy objects such as matzah, the Sefer Torah and the shofar are kept covered for fear of the Satan, but the Megillah is unfolded entirely because it is an iggeres and on Purim there is no accuser.

Esther's 'gather all the Jews' was the answer to Haman's 'scattered and divided', and Shushan keeps Purim with Yerushalayim because its unity made it like Yerushalayim, the city that joins all Jews together.
The haste throughout the Megillah is not incidental: a miracle from a place beyond time cannot fit into the measured pace of time, so it pushes time out of its way.
At Matan Torah earth is raised to heaven, but on Purim heaven comes down to earth; this is why Purim cannot be grasped with an earthly mind and is 'ad d'lo yada'.
In the Megillah's hidden names, the direction and placement of the letters decide whether din or chesed is drawn down, and Esther's reversal of them is the 'v'nahafoch hu' of Purim.
A giver of tzedakah himself forms Hashem's name: the coin is the yud, the five fingers the hei, the arm the vav, and the receiver's hand the last hei.
The halachah that Purim tzedakah is given to anyone who asks mirrors how Hashem gives on Purim: whoever stretches out his hand to Him in true emunah receives.
A seudah eaten 'at night' means one eaten sleepily and without excitement; the Purim seudah must have the character of day, bright and alert.
The Rambam's explanation of 'until he says I want' is read as a statement about the root of every Jewish soul: the coercion only weakens the body's interference so that his true will emerges.
Yom Kippur reaches the level of 'I want' only after climbing through ten days, while Purim reveals it even in Jews who had sinned, which is why Yom Kippur is only 'a day like Purim'.

The order of the Torah, of the tribes and of the months runs from top to bottom: the last letters, Shevet Dan and the month of Adar all correspond to the lowest Jews of the generations before Moshiach.
Keeping Purim in the second Adar, next to Nisan, teaches that even the low Jews of Adar cannot be cut off from their root in Nisan and Bereishis.

The mekalel's mockery of 'stale' bread was a claim that Hashem no longer cares for the lowest Jews; the miracle of the bread staying fresh is the answer, and Haman made the same claim about the Jews in exile.
The less observant a Jew is, the happier he tends to be on Purim, because Purim is the day Hashem turns to the lowest and shows him love.
The Mashgiach compares Purim's clowning and wine to an anesthetic: the remedy Hashem gives on Purim is so strong for the soul that it must be taken without seeing it, and it works regardless.
Rashi's unusual, almost poetic term 'the letter of Purim' signals that the Megillah is a personally addressed letter: each reader must study it as if written to him alone.
The last generation is like the fingernail: formed last and least sensitive, yet once contained in the embryo together with the head, so the end remains bound to the beginning.
Nisan comes from 'nes', a flag on a high pole where Hashem shows Himself, while Adar comes from 'aderes', a cloak; Adar holds as many miracles as Nisan, only concealed.

Adar corresponds to Dan, the tribe at the rear that Amalek attacked because it seemed rejected by Hashem; Amalek is the voice telling a Jew he is lost, and the Megillah and Zachor answer that Hashem forsakes no Jewish soul.
Since the Divine Name has only twelve permutations, Adar Sheni has none and is counted as the 'kolel'; the One who is added is Hashem Himself, who joins Klal Yisrael and makes up whatever is lacking.
Shabbos is felt most by tzaddikim, but Purim is the opposite: it is made for the lowest and most distant, and the lower a person is, the more Purim he has.
History moves not in a straight line but in a circle, so the lowest generation, the heel, is the one that will become the head of all generations.
The name Adar is read as aderes, a cloak: the month in which Hashem is present but wrapped up and unseen, in contrast to Nisan, the month of nissim.

Adar Sheni is an appendage to the calendar just as the last eight pesukim, written by Moshe in tears, are an appendage to the Sefer Torah; both carry the mark of death and forgetting, which is why Haman rejoiced at them.
The greatest nissim are the ones within nature, where each event alone is insignificant and only the timing of all of them together reveals Hashem's hand.

A story like Vashti's refusal, which a yeshiva would dismiss as idle news, turned out to be part of the nes we read every year; so too today's events, even elections, may be part of a future Megillah.

Achashverosh's feast celebrated his calculation that the seventy years were over with no Beis Hamikdash, so taking part in it was a denial of the coming of Moshiach and the geulah, one of the thirteen principles.

The Megillah's light exceeds that of the Torah of Moshe precisely because it was given to a generation that had fallen lowest, with intermarriage like today; one who goes down into a deep pit needs a stronger light.
The Megillah stays even in the days of Moshiach because its real story has not yet been told: it will be the story of the last Purim of galus, which ushers in the geulah.
Adar Sheni is like those who trailed behind the camp outside the clouds of glory; on such a Purim the Shechinah comes down even to those cast out, which makes it a more powerful Purim.
Even if the splitting of the sea had a natural cause, as Graetz claimed, its happening at exactly that moment would be a greater miracle, the kind of hidden miracle the Megillah is made of.
Amalek dared attack right after the splitting of the sea because to him everything is 'mikreh', chance, and Haman, as Mordechai told Esther, carried on that same 'korcha' view.

The angel opposite Memuchan, who is Haman, pleads with the lechem hapanim because Haman's error was the opposite of its lesson: he held that Hashem's love for the rejected had gone cold, while the bread that stayed warm shows that it never does.
The surplus silver used for the protruding hooks, outside the kedushah of the Mishkan, came from the cast-outs of Dan, and Moshe Rabbeinu forgot it because they were forgotten Jews.
The ben ish Mitzri's mockery of the stale lechem hapanim and his claim that Dan's camp was open to him were one position, the same as Amalek's: that the rejected are outside Hashem's love.
The two goats of Yom Kippur must be identical because Yaakov and Esav can look the same, yet Hashem loves Yaakov for the hidden point within him.
Haman matched the main half-shekels but ignored the surplus of the rejected; that overlooked silver, given first, is what nullified his decree.
The Mashgiach suggests that today's Jews are gilgulim of Shevet Dan, so Purim, the Yom Tov of the rejected, is their Yom Tov and grows greater the lower they fall.

The 960 hours of forty full days correspond to the 960 lugin of a mikveh, the measure in which even a whole creature is nullified, so Matan Torah, a rebirth like a mikveh, could not use 'part of the day counts as a whole'.
Adam's sin, the error before the Golden Calf and the error at Achashverosh's feast share one root, not waiting, and Mordechai, who urged the Jews to wait, was a repair of Adam's sin.
The five final letters are letters of din, yet the Midrash calls them letters of redemption; the purpose of din is to be transformed into geulah.

Haman's ten thousand kikar offset only the shekalim of the 600,000; the extra 1775 shekalim, linked to the rejected Jews of Dan, had nothing against them, and so it was they who brought the salvation.
The sum of the whole aleph-beis together with the five final letters is 1775, the number of forgotten shekalim, showing that those outside are still included in Klal Yisrael.
Beyond the Tanya's answer, the Mashgiach adds that the red heifer is prepared outside the camp, unlike a chatas, and so it brings salvation to those who are outside, like the rejected of Dan.
An 'ohr chadash' differs from a new object: new shoes are new for a week, but the light of Purim is new by its essence and remains a surprise every year.
The word 'Megillah' itself means revealing, while Esther points to hiding: on Purim what was hidden becomes revealed.
Haman's war on Mordechai was a contest of reishis: Amalek, the reishis of tumah, tried to reach the fiftieth level of tumah to overpower Mordechai, whose strength also came from reishis.
The miracles of the Megillah were deliberately natural, events the nations could read in the newspapers, because on Purim the heavenly comes down into nature rather than nature rising above itself.
The Megillah must be read from a parchment scroll written in ink because the reading purifies the very materials of nature, animal hide and earthly chemicals, together with the reader's gashmiyus.
Because the world has sunk lower this year, the light of the Megillah must reach deeper than ever, so no one is too low to receive it.
Adar, the last month, mirrors Nisan in reverse: Nisan is named for its open miracles, while Adar means a cloak, the covering of miracles, and its Megillah has none.
The Megillah names Memuchan, Chazal's Haman, only at its start, to signal the reader to watch Haman, because Haman is the one who made the whole Megillah.

Mordechai's greatness had to be designed by Haman: a tzaddik full of rachmanus would have made a painless death for his enemy and asked for little honor or house, while only cruel, honor-seeking Haman knew how to make a fifty-amah gallows, a royal parade and a palace.

The lowest tribe, Dan, produced Chushim, who could not hear or speak, yet he is the one who killed Esav; the Mashgiach links this to the generation before Moshiach, a generation of Chushim and hester panim.

Adar Sheini stands outside the order of the twelve months, like the last eight pesukim of the Torah, which have a separate status; Haman thought the Jews there were outside the camp, but they too belong to it.

Following the Alshich, the Mashgiach reads the apiryon passuk as saying that Hashem, who lacks no silver or gold, wanted the Beis Hamikdash only for the glowing love inside it; that love gave the building a neshama, unlike the cold marble of Rome.

Efron's name comes from afar, earth: when Avraham's shekalim reached his hands their fire had already risen, leaving him cold metal, while 'Machpelah' alludes to Avraham's gift being compounded above.
Yehoash survived six years in the Kodesh HaKadashim because his neshama came from there, from the mitzvah of shekalim, the money of atonement linked to Yom Kippur.
By killing the Kohen Gadol in the Mikdash on Yom Kippur, Yehoash defiled the Kodesh HaKadashim in all three of Sefer Yetzirah's dimensions: place, time and soul.
Because Haman's decree was total annihilation, it could not take effect: the shekel touches the nucleus in every Jew that can never be destroyed.
The equal half-shekel reflects the level where Jews are children rather than servants: a servant can be better or worse as a servant, but a son is never more or less a son.
The Jews' shekalim came before Haman's because theirs are the yud, the first letter and fire, while his are earth, the last; the yud is the tiniest letter but the greatest.

The Mashgiach learns from Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's valley of gold that a Jew's word and desire can create real 'coins', so the heavenly shekalim of every year are made by Jews who yearn to give when they hear Parshas Shekalim.

The Mashgiach reads the Rambam on a coerced 'I want' as a secret of the Jewish heart, not just a halachic device: the beating only subdues the body, and the inner point that always wants Hashem's will comes out.
Shekalim corresponds to the tip of the yud, above the Name itself, the same level the Mashgiach finds in 'lifnei Hashem' of Yom Kippur, where no blemish of sin reaches.

Of all people, Yehoash, who sinned against the Holy of Holies in place, time and soul at once, is the one the haftarah credits with the shekalim, which shows that the inner point of a Jew stays untouched even after such a sin.
A lottery is a fitting vehicle for Yom Kippur and Purim because, like a lottery win, the closeness of every Jew at that root point has no reason that any angel could explain.
Rav told Rabbah bar bar Chanah that paying the workers was the din, not just middas chassidus, because for a person on a higher level a higher standard becomes his law.
Just as an animal has a life-force beyond its body, Amalek has an inner force that cools Jews' emunah, and Parshas Zachor is aimed at that force, not at physical Amalekites.
Every person carries a small piece of Amalek within himself, his own yetzer hara, and the reading of Zachor weakens that inner piece.
Purim is a day to reconcile with Hashem in which the lowest Jew is precious to Him, because the Purim decree came on Jews who had sinned and Hashem nevertheless annulled it.
Holy things are normally kept covered, but the Megillah is spread open on Purim, because Purim's kedushah spreads over the whole world.
Hashem's name is absent from the Megillah not because Purim is lower but because its kedushah is higher than the name Havayah, so the name appears only covered, in initial and final letters.
Adar is read as 'cloak': its miracles are the same as Nissan's, only wrapped in nature, as the fish of the mazal of Adar live hidden under the water.
Achashverosh's swings from one extreme to the other, in his marriages and in his taxes, prove he had no character of his own and was only moved from above.
The absence of Hashem's name from the Megillah reflects the incompleteness of the name while Amalek, whose gematria equals safek, spreads doubt in the world.
Reading the world is like reading an x-ray: to the layman it is meaningless splashes, while the specialist, like the man of emunah, sees exactly what is there.
Learning the Megillah is an exercise: once one can find Hashem's name between its lines, one can do the same with the New York Times.
Once Hashem is found, as in the Ba'al Shem Tov's hide-and-seek, He no longer needs to hide, and the finding itself is the joy of Purim.
Adar corresponds to Eilam, Persia, whose name means hiddenness ('ta'alumah'); Hashem 'set His throne in Eilam', and so the Purim miracle came hidden inside a story of nature.
The seventy-year decree torn up by amen yehei shmei rabbah echoes the seventy years of galus Bavel, whose darkest last stretch under Persia is the time of Purim.

The two halves of the Name match heaven and earth (the initials of 'yismechu hashamayim vesagel ha'aretz'); in heaven Hashem is seen, but on earth Amalek can hide Him behind the cloak of nature and chance.
Torah festivals are mentioned in Retzeh, the avodah, while Chanukah and Purim belong to Modim, where one bows down, because they bring holiness to the lowest places and the lowest Jews.
Levels of Jews mirror the days: the one who only learns is like Shabbos, one who works only as needed is like Yom Tov, then Chol Hamoed, then the weekday.
'Le'olam chasdo' means His kindness is hidden ('olam' from 'ne'elam'), and 'dor vador' means tumbling down, the emunah rolling down through the generations to the very last before Moshiach.
The precise Rambam's words 'many books' teach that the prohibition is not limited to a few books of idolatry but reaches all reading that plants doubts in emunah.
The Mashgiach explains that Canaan corresponds to chesed precisely because in the sitra achra the male side is subdued ('nichna'), the reverse of holiness, where gevurah yields to chesed.
The kri/ksiv of 'iro' shows the hidden tziruf of Adar: only because the word ends with heh is the Name complete, hinting that in Adar the male yields to the female.

The Gemara's 'Memuchan is Haman' and the Midrash's 'Memuchan is Daniel' do not conflict: Daniel, the soul of redemption, ruled for the heavenly court that the right side prevail, and Haman ruled the same thing below.

Rabbi Yehuda's simanim for the plagues follow his view that chametz must be burned: as the soul of Yehuda, corresponding to fire, the root of all elements, he insists on reaching the root, the initials.

Har HaBayis, bought from Aravnah, whose name begins with the letters of 'or' (the element of fire), and Me'aras HaMachpelah, bought from Efron, whose name spells 'afar' (earth), are Israel's 'reishis' and 'acharis', and both hold the same Adam and Avos.
Moshe's name is missing from Tetzaveh, read in the week of his yahrzeit, because Moshe takes a different name in each generation; in Haman's time he was Mordechai.
Mishloach manos makes all Jewish families one, like an eruv chatzeiros, where a shared meal unites separate households, and Amalek's power of mockery cannot bear such unity.
Shmuel's opening 'Hashem sent me to anoint you king' is not a preface but the condition for the war: only one who includes all of Klal Yisrael can fight Amalek, who includes all impurity.

Shaul's sparing of the animals came from humility, not desire: not believing he was king, he tried to acquire the all-including power through korbanos on the mizbeach in Binyamin's portion, turning the war into a preparation for the mizbeach.
Binyamin's stone on the choshen lacks the letters of the avos precisely because Binyamin is himself the unity of Israel, the place of the mizbeach.
The donations of the nesi'im, the shoham and milu'im stones, were of the aspect of the months and shevatim rather than of Shabbos, unlike every other gift to the Mishkan.

Haman's lottery read Adar as weak, Binyamin's month without the names of the avos and the month of Moshe's death, but in Adar Sheni the all-including power was present through Mordechai, a spark of Moshe, and through Binyamin's mizbeach.
Reading the Megillah 'backwards' means reading it as past history; one who does so does not fulfill the mitzvah, because its salvations happen again each year at the reading.
The Purim seudah is like taking a medicine or vitamin: each bite brings in the strength of the renewed acceptance of Torah, since Mordechai instituted it.

The Mashgiach reads the Megillah's double name as a key: a sefer is written for anyone who buys it, but an iggeres is addressed to one person, so every Jew should feel that the Megillah was written to him, the way a son feels news from home.

He contrasts the Megillah with lofty mitzvos that are covered, like the shofar, the matzos and the Sefer Torah, of which only the column being read is opened: the Megillah is spread open entirely, because it reveals what is hidden and spreads its lights through the world.
Since Purim's nature is to descend, the lowness of the generation is no obstacle but the reverse: the lower the generation, the greater its Purim, and the greater Mordechai becomes.
He explains Hashem's special love for Esther as His love for a generation that serves Him in hiddenness, without the sweetness earlier generations felt, and says such service merits keser malchus.
Citing R' Yitzchak of Vorka, he identifies the earlier days on which the Megillah may be read as the three days of preparation before Purim's kabbalas haTorah of love, as before Shavuos.
He explains the custom of disguising oneself on Purim from the fact that Purim's lights, greater in one respect than Shabbos, come down clothed and hidden.
The Megillah writes 'turning over' twice, for the day and for the month, so the whole month carries the power of reversal, including a person turning his own ways around.
The three days before Purim on which the Megillah could once be read are three days of preparation, as before Shavuos, since Purim is a receiving of the Torah with love.
'Yom Kippurim' is read as 'a day like Purim', not the reverse, showing that Purim is the greater day.
Food, unlike other mitzvos, enters the body and becomes part of the person, which is why each Yom Tov has a food that lets a Jew carry the day's holiness with him after it ends.
A Sefer Torah is kept covered because it is holy, but the Megillah, holier still, is opened entirely, since 'Megillah' comes from revealing and its holiness must spread over the world.
The great tzaddikim could not ask for the geulah on Purim because then they were shown that galus is not mere punishment but has tikkunim still to be done.
Haman chose Adar thinking Moshe's merit ended with his death, but for Jews 'death of Moshe' does not exist: a Yehoshua always follows to carry the Torah, so Moshe's influence never ends.

The stragglers whom Amalek struck were cast out by the cloud and called 'not fearing G-d' by the passuk, yet precisely for them Hashem declares eternal war on Amalek, which shows how dear even such a Jew is.
Purim, unlike other Yamim Tovim, needs no preparation because it came by lot, and a lot reveals what is one's own without effort: the Jew's bond to Hashem, who chose him as His portion.
The Megillah is called an iggeres because it is a personal letter from the King to each Jew by name, and the further a Jew is, the more it is addressed to him.
Drinking on Purim is needed because the holiness revealed then is too great to receive in a conscious state, just as some things can only be borne under anesthesia.
The two mentions of 'once a year' at the end of Tetzaveh hint at two atonements: the avodah of Yom Kippur and Purim's 'avodah without avodah', a Yom Tov made for the stragglers.

Aharon earned the choshen, which carries the judgment of Bnei Yisrael on the heart, because he rejoiced in his younger brother's greatness; only one without personal interest can hold Klal Yisrael in his heart.
Purim did not only add another holy day to the calendar like Shabbos and the Yamim Tovim; it brought into being a new world above that had never existed, the root of Mordechai's soul.

Yom Kippur and Purim reach the same world of yechidah from opposite directions: on Yom Kippur Jews leave the world and rise like angels, while on Purim the light descends into eating and drinking and sanctifies the body.

The Yom Kippur requirement to make peace with others before the day is not only a separate obligation: without becoming one soul with all Jews one simply has no Yom Kippur, and the same holds for Purim.
The word 'mikra' in the blessing on the Megillah is read as 'calling': the blessing is a summons to the hidden light of the Megillah to come down.
The halachah that the Megillah is spread out fully and folded rather than rolled reflects its essence: it is the revelation of what was hidden, the light concealed above becoming revealed.
Purim wine and Purim tzedakah are a different kind of wine and tzedakah, just as an esrog that costs little before Sukkos becomes a precious mitzvah object when Sukkos arrives.
A miracle cloaked in nature is not smaller than the splitting of the sea but greater, since Hashem achieved the salvation without needing to change nature at all.
The months descend from Nissan to Adar just as the generations descend toward the end of days; our era is the Adar of history, in which the miracles are as real as ever but hidden.
The word 'happened' does not belong in a Jew's dictionary: calling events chance is itself the 'karcha' of Amalek, which cooled the warmth of Jewish faith.
Hamelech, kes and Haman share the gematria 95: Haman's presence is what forces the Megillah to say 'the King' instead of Hashem's name.
The pshat and the derash of 'the King' do not conflict: the verse means Achashverosh, but Achashverosh acted as he did because the King above pulled the strings.
Yom Kippur and Purim are opposites in direction: on Yom Kippur we rise to Hashem, while on Purim Hashem descends to the lowest levels and holiness enters nature itself.
Reading the Megillah backwards, as an old story from long ago, is not fulfilling the mitzvah, because the Megillah happens anew every year when Adar and Purim come.
Purim was created in galus, so in some ways Purim is better in galus than in Eretz Yisroel; Purim of the walled cities belongs to higher levels than Purim made for those outside them.
Every Jew in galus is a shliach, and his home on 16th Avenue or 42nd Street is like a Chabad house; the "converts" the Jews are exiled to gather are sparks of holiness.
When prophecy ended, Purim began a new era: ruach hakodesh today means arriving at the truth in the Gemara and in halachah through clear learning.
Simcha is the test of learning: one who seeks Hashem in the Gemara feels joy, and one who feels none was not seeking Hashem's will in his learning.
Torah is of the mind and tefillah of the heart; just as a hole in the heart or the brain makes a creature treif, a person needs both Torah and tefillah to live with deveikus.
Deveikus is for everyone: learning even a piece of Chumash with Rashi with taste and vitality is deveikus at one's own level.
Purim Meshulash and Shabbos Erev Pesach always come together: when Purim falls on Friday, Erev Pesach falls on Shabbos, so Purim Meshulash carries the geulah kevius of the Imrei Noam.

The Mashgiach reads 'velo ya'avor' through the moon: the second half of the month is Eisav's domain, so Purim, the wiping out of Amalek, cannot cross into it until Moshiach, just as Edom told Yisrael 'lo sa'avor bi'.
The Sunday seudah of Purim Meshulash, held on the sixteenth, is the one time in decades that the Jews step into Eisav's domain.
Hillel's rise to the nesius on a Shabbos Erev Pesach, a nesius of Beis Dovid, was itself a sign of Moshiach ben David on that kevius.
R' Chezkel of Kuzmir's claim that Moshiach would come in his weaker generation is no joke: less is expected of later generations, whose trials are greater.
Since Torah and tefillah must enter through the mouth, a mouth soiled by forbidden speech blocks them; the Pesach mitzvos of eating and telling purify the mouth so that 'Toras Hashem' may be in it.
The lowest generation is the 'heel' of Moshiach, and its very lowness is its task: Moshiach comes to the lowest generation.
Jews who are not yet worthy can 'borrow' from their future: because they will be good, they may already call Hashem 'Father' now, and this was Esther's plea for salvation that very day.
A large alef is seen from afar, a small alef only from close up: in Adar's hiddenness the call of love seems absent, but once one is brought near through Purim one sees it was there all along.

The hooks of the pillars, made from the forgotten extra silver, stood outside the holy courtyard; they are the forgotten Jews, who are still destined to be fastened to the great pillars of Torah and chessed.
The extra Jews are linked to the forgetting of Torah, and Rabbi Akiva's soul, the root of pilpul, could account for them, because sharp Torah study can recover even what fell to the fiftieth gate.
Like a diamond given up to save a life that then lives on in every descendant, Moshe's Mishkan was not lost: its holiness took the wrath meant for Israel and keeps the people alive.
Hashem's Name is concealed in the Megillah because its light comes from a hidden world that cannot be revealed outward, and the reading of the Megillah is what calls that light down.
Esther wanted only kindness, but Hashem agreed only in part: Purim needed both chassadim for Israel and judgment on Haman, so her words carry the Name both ways.
The Mashgiach reads the Rema's switch from 'mishteh vesimcha' to 'yarbeh ketzas biseudah' as deliberate: the Rema is not adopting the Ran's obligation but the feast every view agrees to.

The Mashgiach distinguishes two dinim of joy: the Magen Avraham's general yom tov for a miracle, which can be kept in any way, and Purim's own mishteh, a remembrance of a miracle that came through wine, which requires wine.
Chanukah has no din of mishteh vesimcha despite the kal vachomer of Hallel, which shows that Purim's feasting is not derived from that kal vachomer.
The Rema's rule not to go against a minhag applies where one visibly opposes it; since Jews always drink l'chaim, a little wine at the meal does not visibly break the custom.
The joy of Adar was taught by the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas because his family, descended from Haman, became Jews only through the Purim miracle.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach separates the joy of Purim, which is the core obligation of remembering the miracle, from the seudah and gifts, which the Sages only added as its form.
The Mashgiach reads the Yerushalmi's moving of a Shabbos Purim seudah to Sunday as proof that the joy of Purim is a distinct joy that may not be mixed with another.

Joining Rashi's comparison of the twenty-four books to a kallah's adornments with the Megillah, the Mashgiach says Megillas Esther itself became a kallah, so the joy of the Megillah is a kallah's joy.

With the mashal of a king whose kallah is found in a disgraceful place, the Mashgiach explains that it is no disgrace for the king to go to her, since she is his kallah; so the joy of Purim is Hashem's closeness to the Jewish people even in their lowest state.

Every substance carries a fixed measure of spiritual 'units' set at creation, so a half-shekel of silver holds exactly enough love to arouse Hashem's love in return, like the five sela'im of pidyon haben.

The letters of 'barech' show doubling in the ones, tens and hundreds, and blessing reaches its full measure at a hundredfold; this is why the hundred kikar of shekalim, given in Adar, became ten thousand.
Haman gave a hundred times what the Jews gave in order to capture the power of the number one hundred, but the Jews had already preceded him with a hundred kikar given generously.
Yehoash's soul is rooted in Parshas Shekalim, so his life, saved by the Kodesh HaKodashim despite his later sin there, is itself the explanation of what Shekalim is: a place no sin can blemish.
Haman took a beam from the Kodesh HaKodashim for the gallows because his war was against the innermost point of the Jews, and that very beam took revenge on him.
Haman's slander that the Jews were 'asleep from mitzvos' could reach the lower letters of the Name in a Jew's soul, but not the yud and its tip, which precede them.
The name Yehoash contains the letters yud-hei-vav of the Name together with 'esh', fire, the element of the yud and of the coin of fire shown to Moshe.
The Mashgiach reads Moshe's forgetting of the extra shekels as a sign of where they came from: they were given by the 'forgotten' souls outside the camp, so the forgetting itself belongs to them.
The hooks made from the outsiders' silver hung partly outside the holy courtyard yet held the curtains to the pillars, just as those Jews stand outside yet remain bound to the camp.
Haman priced the Jews by the shekalim of the 600,000 alone, repeating Amalek's error of thinking the sinning Jews outside the camp no longer count before Hashem.

Adar Sheni, the thirteenth month that has no permutation of Hashem's name, corresponds to the Jews expelled beyond the twelve tribes' camps, which is why Adar is the 'forgotten' month that Haman's lottery found.

Rabbi Akiva, who expounded the crowns of the letters that are shaped like hooks, is the one who reminded Moshe of the hooks of the pillars, and his name hints at 'ikvesa d'Meshicha', the last generations.
Parshas Zachor must be read from the scroll precisely because its message, that no Jew is cut off, has to be fully understood with all its derashos by every Jew.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Megillah opens with Achashverosh's feast to show that Hashem began the salvation in the very midst of the Jews' sin.
The seven ministers of Achashverosh had names that alluded to korbanos, so that their heavenly counterparts, the seven angels with the same names, could plead for the Jews in Vashti's judgment.
The angels' concern with the leap year was, at root, the moon's repair: Esther is the moon, and her kingship restores the moon's rule.
The moon's jealousy of the sun is the root of the narrow eye in the world, which leads through the sin of the Tree of Knowledge and Kayin to the sale of Yosef and the exile.
The number thirteen ties the repairs together: the thirteenth month, the thirteenth middah of seeing another's good, and the thirteenth year of Yosef in prison and of Rabbi Shimon in the cave.
Lag BaOmer and Purim are a pair: 'sheves achim gam yachad' of Rabbi Shimon and the gathering of all the Jews on Purim are one repair of the sale of Yosef.

The Mashgiach parallels soul and time: just as the souls before Moshiach are the 'heels' of the generations, Adar, the month furthest from Nisan, is the 'heels' of the year, with the same inner G-dliness under more garments.
Adar Sheini is read as hester upon hester: just when it seems Adar is over and Nisan has come, another Adar begins.
The custom of dressing up on Purim teaches that garments mean nothing: a Jew is not fooled by someone dressed as Haman or Achashverosh, for behind everything stands Hashem.

David's sparing of Shimi, which seemed to cause the decree, was really the root of the rescue: because David saw Hashem's name even in Shimi's curse, measure for measure Mordechai descended from Shimi and revealed that Haman is nothing.
The very existence of the Jewish people proclaims morality, and this, the Mashgiach says, is what arouses the nations' hatred.
Yaakov blessed Naftali not with a virtue but with swiftness; Adar is Naftali's month, so in Adar things change quickly, and speed itself is a sign of Hashem's hand.

The Mashgiach reads the Rema's switch from 'mishteh v'simcha' to 'add a little to the meal' as deliberate: the seudah is not Mordechai's enactment, which the custom rejects, but a thanksgiving meal on the model of a private miracle day, so it fulfils the stringent view without uprooting the minhag.
The leap month is the moon, Knesses Yisroel, catching up with the sun, Hashem, and Purim Katan belongs to the 'small luminary' that rules the night.
Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim opens with 'shivisi Hashem l'negdi tamid' and its last halachos, those of Purim Katan, close with 'v'tov lev mishteh tamid': the two 'tamid's frame a Jew's whole day.
Because no one commands it, Purim Katan can accomplish more than Purim itself: an uncommanded thanks offered in the darkness of hester panim gives Hashem special nachas.

The Midrash's 'we will rejoice in Him' teaches that rejoicing with Hashem does not depend on a day set aside with halachos, so even a day the calendar does not demand can be filled with joy in Hashem.
The final, added month can repair what was lacking in all the months before it, making the end of the year a renewal like a new creation.
The Megillah has two faces: all year it is on the level of Kesuvim, and on Purim it receives a new light; this is why a Megillah written among the Kesuvim is invalid.
For the Megillah to be written above the level of Kesuvim, Esther had to be one of the seven prophetesses.
The Mashgiach reads 'lechalosam' in the days of Haman as 'to His kallah': like a king who goes to his bride in a disgraceful place, Hashem comes to Klal Yisroel even in its lowest state.
The bracha 'al mikra megillah' equals 'chosson v'kallah' in gematria, because the Megillah reveals Klal Yisroel as Hashem's kallah.
On Purim Katan the Megillah is read in the heavenly yeshiva that follows Rabbi Eliezer b'Rabbi Yosi, and on Purim a Jew can enter the heichal of whichever tanna he wishes.
A small avodah of a Jew today, such as washing negel vasser, may bring Hashem more nachas than the great mesiras nefesh of earlier generations.

The Mashgiach reads the dispute about feasting on Adar I in light of the Magen Avraham: even if Mordechai and Esther instituted nothing for Adar I, the general duty to commemorate a miracle remains, and so cannot simply be pushed off to Adar II.

He suggests that the dispute over Adar I may parallel the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rava on whether Hallel is required on Purim: if no Hallel is required, as Rava holds, there may also be no duty to commemorate.
He explains Pharaoh's doubled dream as the model for Purim: a second time does not add a new thing but fixes and strengthens the first.
Like fire, which rises because it does not belong to this world, Purim's lights belong to a place above this world and tend to go back up, so they must be held with 'iron grips' through repetition.
Esther's delay to a second feast is explained as her understanding that the Purim she was creating needed a repetition to take hold.
Because the thirteenth month is a deeper darkness than the twelfth, a leap year's Purim must lift Jews from a greater lowliness, which is why it needs two Purims together.

The Mashgiach reads 'one who reads the Megillah backwards has not fulfilled his obligation' as aimed at one who sees Purim only as a past event and does not know that its miracles come down today, and that the main Purim is just before Moshiach.

Since Esther is hinted in 'haster astir', which the Torah says of the end of days, the deeper the hiddenness near the end, the stronger the Purim; this is why the present generation has a greater Purim than earlier ones.

The first petichta of the Midrash on the Megillah, about cutting off Babylon, seems unrelated to the Purim story; the Mashgiach explains that it speaks of the last and greatest Purim, when Babylon is clothed in Amalek and is finally destroyed.

Achashverosh is called a king who ruled 'by himself' to show that a ruler through whom salvation comes to the Jews is appointed by Hashem and not chosen by the people, just as the Torah had to be given by compulsion and not only because the Jews wanted it.
Haman's whole power was fear, and 'v'nahafoch' means turning that fear back onto the enemy, as in 'tipol aleihem eimasa vafachad'.
The Mashgiach notes that the Gemara speaks of sleep, not eating, in connection with bitachon: Chizkiyahu's sleep on the night Sancheriv surrounded Yerushalayim showed his emunah.

The Mashgiach compares remembering a miracle to reading Parshas Zachor each year: the remembrance must come within a span in which it would otherwise be forgotten, so a year with two Adars seemingly needs the celebration already in the first Adar.
He separates the general duty to celebrate a miracle from the specific Purim law of drinking wine, instituted because the miracle came through wine; Purim Katan has the first but not the second.
By this distinction the Mashgiach reads the Rema's wording precisely: on Purim Katan he does not speak of a 'mishteh v'simcha' but of adding somewhat to the meal as a remembrance of the miracle.
The deeper joy of Purim Katan is the acceptance of the Torah with love on Purim, a joy so great that a Jew cannot wait with it until Purim Gadol.
He reads Boaz's 'vayitav libo' as joy in Torah study, linking the 'good heart' of Boaz to the Rema's 'a good heart is a constant feast' on Purim Katan.

The Mashgiach reads the Chasam Sofer's account as proof that joining redemption to redemption is not a law at all: Haman, who knew the calendar, was not concerned with a Torah or rabbinic law, only with keeping salvation away, so it must be a segulah.

Because the second Adar was chosen only for the salvation Jews need in galus, the Mashgiach suggests that in the days of Moshiach, when Purim is only a remembrance, the reason of not passing over mitzvos will prevail and Purim of a leap year will be in Adar Rishon.
The day is called Purim Katan, not Purim Rishon like Pesach Rishon, because Adar Rishon belongs to the small luminary, the moon, and is the month that fills in its diminution.

The Mashgiach traces a chain of jealousy from the moon's diminution: the brothers against Yosef, the spies, and the rivalry of the kingdom of the House of David with that of Yosef, all of which Moshiach will heal.
Esther is the moon, and since the whole Purim story grows out of the moon's diminution, her counsel to gather all the Jews was the way to fill it in.
Shaul's merit of hiding his kingship, out of lowliness, is what brought forth Mordechai, who had the same lowliness; to such a person Hashem stands at his right hand.
The 300 killed in Shushan on the second day were new Amalekites: men with a finer spark of Amalek who would not count as Amalek for a simple Jew but do for the higher Jew of Shushan Purim.

Mordechai left Jerusalem for Shushan to raise Esther because his light could be revealed only in a place of hester panim, planting for all generations the power of hidden Jews to bind themselves to the light of Purim.
In Shushan the light is called Shoshanah rather than Esther: Esther is hiddenness, while Shoshanah is the rose that blooms openly in its beauty.

Mordechai's two answers in the Targum do not contradict: bowing to Haman as the controller of one's livelihood is idolatry in the higher tractate of Avodah Zarah, and Haman's image 'from behind' is even a passing thought that someone other than Hashem gives one's bread.

Mordechai turned the slave-for-bread claim around: it is not Haman who gives him bread but he who gives Haman bread, since all blessing comes down first to Israel and only through them to the nations.
The seudah of Shushan Purim is a seudas bris milah: both remove the orlah and reveal the holy point, giving a glimmer of the days of Moshiach.

Esther named Shushan only because Achashverosh would never grant a Yom Tov for Jerusalem, knowing that Shushan would vanish while Jerusalem, the one place that is certainly a walled city, would remain.
Achashverosh thought Vashti was killed on Pesach, but the wise men told him the day was Shushan Purim, so the Megillah's miracle both begins and ends on Shushan Purim.

The Chasam Sofer's reading of the decree on the day of the omer waving (the war on Amalek on erev Pesach, the Beis Hamikdash that night) explains why the kings who feared its rebuilding celebrated only after Pesach passed.
Shaul counted the people with sheep because they were the Pesach lambs to be offered right after the war on erev Pesach.
Building on the Ruzhiner, the Mashgiach explains that Shmuel's night-long cry was a tefillah that Shaul's plan, sparing Agag so Haman and Purim would come, should succeed.
The Satan blocks with 'water' precisely what decides the eternity of Israel: he did so at the Akeidah, which answered Yishmael, and again when Mordechai went to gather the Jews.
Today's exile, with its politics, parties and elections, is itself the Satan's great 'water', and the mesiras nefesh of Mordechai's cry is what lets Jews pass through it.
The Satan of Yishmael hates wine because he knows his downfall will come when Jews drink wine on Purim.
Kaddish is said in Aramaic, the language of the 'back side' of holiness, because its whole content is that Hashem's kingship be revealed even in the place of the sitra achra.
The Megillah has a 'second Targum' because it belongs to Adar, the last month, which itself has a second Adar beyond the order of months: its light reaches even lower.
A large part of the Targum Sheni, seemingly unrelated to the Megillah, speaks about Shlomo Hamelech, because like the Megillah he went down into the lowest places to reveal Hashem's kingship.
Esther's messenger to Mordechai was a shed, which explains the plural 'vayagidu', the plural of the 'others' of the sitra achra, and why Mordechai had to go into water after speaking with it.

Yaakov left Lavan's deepest sparks because the lowest klipah holds the highest sparks; he could repair them only at Gilad, the place of Eliyahu, where 'yegar sahadusa' equals 'malchuso bakol mashalah' in gematria.
The 'yekar' of the Megillah's Targum equals 'ketzeh ha'am' and 'pisgam' equals 'chodesh Adar' in gematria: the Megillah's Targum speaks to those who have fallen to the edge of the camp.
Shushan Purim, the Purim of walled Yerushalayim, is the day of the final letter tzaddik, the future redemption, which is why Yerushalayim's 'wall of fire' is tied to it.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Megillah is the same Torah of Moshe accepted willingly rather than under compulsion, and so it reveals greater light and will be understood ever more in the future.

Ezra's writing 'and he died' of Hadar, and his listing Mordechai as having fallen, have one root: his book records things at the level of his prophecy, which does not reach the world of the eighth king to which Mordechai belonged.
Wisdom can grasp beyond prophecy, yet as long as Amalek is in the world nothing more can be grasped; Mordechai, living after Amalek's eradication, could reach further.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof from the end of the verse, 'lo yasuf', rather than its beginning, reflects the higher level of Shushan Purim, while the beginning of the verse reflects Purim as it is understood today and as Ezra understood it.
The Mashgiach reads 'malkah' in 'Esther HaMalkah wrote' as ruach hakodesh, not political rank: her authority over the Chachamim came from prophecy, not from the throne.

The verse about Achashverosh's tax, which seems to interrupt Esther's dialogue with the Chachamim, is the premise of her answer: he was no king, so the 'kings of Madai and Paras' are Mordechai and Esther.
A Jewish king is a giver of kedushah and a king of the nations is a taker; Achashverosh, who levies a tax, loses the vav of giving from his name, as Efron did.
Shlomo HaMelech, who ruled the world without war, is a model of the future Yerushalayim that will need no physical wall because Hashem will be its wall of fire.
The Jews of Shushan, who had sinned more, received a greater day precisely because nothing remained in them but the indestructible inner point of Yerushalayim.
The Mashgiach reads 'kosel' as the Name of Hashem together with 'tel', a ruin: even in destruction the Name is there, and so the Kosel Maaravi in every Jew's heart can never be destroyed.

The Midrash and the Zohar on Yaakov's bowing are both true: each speaks from its own world, and Yaakov, who knew both, chose to accept a flaw in the world of drush for a far greater tikun in the world of sod.
The Gemara's unflattering names for Devorah and Chulda do not fault them personally; they mark a time when the world was out of order, with din ruling over chesed.
The first letters, 'let every man rule in his house', were not a foolish decree but the very beginning of the miracle, reversing the order of din over chesed.

The Megillah has two statuses: all year it is one of the books of Kesuvim, but on Purim it becomes an iggeres of the world of tikun, so that being written together with the other books is a disgrace to it.
The word iggeres, spelled out in full, equals in gematria 'yom shekulo Shabbos', the day that is entirely Shabbos, for Mordechai belonged to that future world.
Because Mordechai repaired the world of drush, the Gemara expounds the Megillah verse by verse from beginning to end, and the Megillah itself ends with 'doresh tov l'amo'.

Flax, called 'bad' in the holy tongue because each stalk rises 'bad bevad', alone, embodies separation; that is why Rav objected to planting it on Purim, the day of gathering, and why flax could be used for holiness only in the Beis HaMikdash.
The descent of the Megillah into the Persian chronicles is the opposite of the Greek translation of the Torah: what there brought darkness here brought 'light and joy' to the Jews.

The Baal HaTanya's parable of the jewel poured out over the ill prince explains why the highest, previously hidden Torah was spread widely despite the risk of disgrace: some of it will reach and revive the prince.

The Mashgiach applies the same parable to the Megillah: its light, greater than at Matan Torah, was poured into Achashverosh's feast and the Persian chronicles for the sake of the prince, the Jewish people in hiding.

Esther's fate and the Megillah's fate are one: just as Esther, the soul of the Jewish people, was lost in Achashverosh's palace, so the light of the Torah went down into a Megillah without Hashem's name.

The Chasam Sofer models the ten sons of Haman on Moshe, Aharon and Miriam: as each of the three gifts passed to the survivor until all ended with Moshe, so each son's power passed to the next until everything collapsed with Vayzasa.
The odd wording 'v'lo ya'avor' ('it shall not pass') rather than 'it shall not be added' hints at Esav's words 'lo sa'avor bi': the sixteenth of Adar is Esav's border, which Purim cannot cross.

Esther asked for 'tomorrow' as well, yet could not ask for the sixteenth and seventeenth, because asking for that would mean asking for the waning of the moon itself to be undone, which belongs to the perfected world.

The lower seven sons of Haman stand against the seven shepherds, so Vayzasa, the last, stands against Dovid HaMelech; just as nachash has the numerical value of Moshiach, the Mashgiach suggests Vayzasa is the counterpart of Moshiach ben Dovid.

Moshe Rabbeinu's last words, 'v'atah al bamoseimo tidroch', were what Mordechai answered Haman when he stepped on him, a hint that in the footsteps of Moshiach the Jews will tread on Haman completely.

The Mashgiach explains why a goral reveals what reason cannot: wealth from business or an inheritance has an understandable cause, but winning by lot has none, so the lot reaches the root that only Hashem knows.

By the angels' own logic they were right to oppose Menashe's teshuvah; Hashem did not overrule them openly but made a hidden tunnel, because the inner point of a Jew cannot be explained to pure intellect.

Haman's lot, meant for destruction, registered above as a judgment 'by lot', and so it moved the case to the one court where the Jews could only be found meritorious: what Haman did below aroused its counterpart above.

The Mashgiach notes that 'hipil pur hu hagoral' has the gematria of 'Moshiach ben David': Haman's lot aroused the world of Moshiach, when the inner purpose of creation, that Yisrael rose first in Hashem's thought, will be revealed.
'Arur Haman' and 'baruch Mordechai' share a gematria because at the inner point all Jews are equal, like the future circle dance of the tzaddikim, where no one stands nearer or farther.

Rashi's unusually sharp word 'mistake' against those who say terumah can be redeemed reflects that Jews are Hashem's terumah; a view that terumah can be exchanged echoes the claim that the Jews can be replaced by another nation.
Tarshish, the stone of Asher, has the same gematria as 'reishis goyim Amalek': Haman wanted the title 'first', which belongs to Yisrael as 'reishis tevuaso', to pass to Amalek.

The Ba'al HaTanya's mezuzos differed from another man's not in the sofer's kavanos but only in being written on the fifteenth, the full moon, which shows what Esther sought in a Purim on the fifteenth.
The fourteenth is a preparation, a 'seat', for Shushan Purim: the Purim of the weaker Jews came through the goral, but one who uses it properly is lifted from it into the fifteenth, which is earned.

The Mashgiach suggests that the spark of holiness in Haman, which the Arizal says must be kept alive on Purim, is Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, a descendant of Zeresh, and that this is why one may 'confuse' and bless Zeresh.

The tannaim's seder in Bnei Brak, which lasted until the time of the morning kriyas shema, came to repair the blemish of Haman's descendants there, whose grandmother Zeresh had advised stopping the morning kriyas shema.
Haman was hanged on the day of the omer harvest because that day begins the count to fifty, the level he tried to seize; and kriyas shema, by gematria, is that same day.

Even the suffix of Hashem's Name may not be erased; the lowest Jews of the last generation are attached to the 'kem' of 'Elokeichem', and Amalek, who tried to erase what may not be erased, is erased measure for measure.

The Gemara's question why Purim is not extended to the sixteenth and seventeenth is a tefillah that the geulah come, when Esav's border will be crossed and those days too will hold the victory over Amalek.
The fiftieth day, being above time, can stretch to include the fifty-first, so Shavuos can be called the time of the giving of the Torah even on the view that it was given on the fifty-first day.
Like a page of Gemara learned on Sunday and reviewed on Monday, which is one page and not two, Adar Sheni is a review of Adar Rishon, so a leap year still has only thirty days of Adar.
Since zrizin makdimin is not pushed off for a hiddur, Adar Rishon must carry a Torah-level remembrance of the miracle, and the prohibition of eulogy and fasting on Purim Katan is that remembrance.
The Chachamim deliberately did not make the festive gathering of Purim a mitzvah, knowing Jews would rejoice on their own, because doing it unbidden is what acceptance with love means.

The leap year is read as the moon's chase after the sun: each year Knesses Yisrael falls further behind in its longing to unite with Hashem, until Adar Sheni evens the two out, which makes Purim in Adar Sheni of a wholly different kind.

Every Tanna has his own heichal in Heaven where one learns as he holds; just as one who never wore Rabbeinu Tam's tefillin will not be admitted to Rabbeinu Tam's heichal, so in Rabbi Yosi's heichal the Megillah is read in Adar Rishon.
The Megillah is read in Heaven on Purim Katan even when Jews below do not read it, so the lights of Purim come down on Purim Katan as well.
Adar Rishon, the time of distance, is itself a month of hester panim, and Purim Katan is when that concealment is broken.
The moon's shorter year (about 355 days against the sun's 365) is itself a second diminution of Knesses Yisrael, besides the diminution of its light.
The leap year is the moon catching up with the sun: Adar Sheni is where they become equal, so Adar Rishon, just before, is the height of hiddenness.

Every Tanna has his own heichal in heaven where Torah is practiced by his view; just as one who never wore Rabbeinu Tam's tefillin is not admitted to Rabbeinu Tam's heichal, there is a mesivta of Rabbi Yosi where the Megillah is read in Adar Rishon.
The Mishnah's passive 'Megillah nikreis' hints that on Purim Katan the Megillah is read in heaven even when Jews below do not read it.
Adar Rishon is the month of hester panim, alluded to in the Gemara's question where Esther is hinted at in the Torah, and the Megillah read in heaven on Purim Katan breaks that hiddenness.
Purim is a new kabbalas haTorah, something the Jews did not attain even at Matan Torah.
Rabbi Meir did not write the Megillah from memory in the ordinary sense: he saw the Megillah written in creation itself, so he was copying from what he saw.
The 'skin' (or) covering creation is what hides its inner Torah; Rabbi Meir saw through it, and that is why his Torah read 'or' with an aleph, light.
Ezra's writing 'and he died' by the eighth king reflects his level of prophecy, not his wisdom; in wisdom he could grasp more than he saw in prophecy, as Rabbi Akiva could expound what Moshe saw.

Rav Yosef's rule that Torah study is greater than saving lives is true, yet Mordechai did not fall: those who separated from him judged by their own level, whose portion was the plain meaning of Torah.
Having one's portion only in the plain meaning of Torah is no lack: the Lechovitcher told such a student he was greater than others, it was simply his portion.

Each word of tefillah is a heichal, a chamber of the King, and davening is passing from one heichal into the next; feeling one has said many chapters without knowing what he said is a sign of being pushed out of the heichalos.
Esther's thirty days of feeling unable to say a warm word before Hashem were the preparation for 'vatilbash Esther malchus', the moment on which the whole miracle of Purim rested.
Esther's 'I have not been called' parallels Avraham sitting at the opening of the tent: he felt he was still outside and could not enter, and precisely then Hashem appeared to him.
A Jew who feels that his words accomplish nothing is precisely the one who can merit the heichal of the Shechinah.

According to the second approach, Esther saw the king's not calling her during the thirty days before Pesach as siyata dishmaya for preparing in purity, and Mordechai's 'al tedami venafshech' meant that even holy personal preparation must give way when Klal Yisroel needs a yeshuah.
The Mashgiach remarks that Shushan Purim, too, is a yom tov for all Jews, even where the megillah is not read, since there are two days of Purim.

Just as a dead animal has every limb of a living one and lacks only its life, every thing, Amalek included, has an inner life-force, and Parshas Zachor targets that life-force rather than Amalek's body.
The Mashgiach notes that Amalek has the numerical value of 'safek', doubt, which is how Amalek's power cools a Jew's emunah.
The two verses about erasing Amalek, 'timcheh' in Ki Seitzei and 'emcheh' in Beshalach, show that our part is to weaken him while the full erasure belongs to Hashem in the days of Moshiach.
Holy things are kept covered so the forces of harm do not envy them, yet the whole Megillah is opened, because Purim's holiness spreads out over the whole world.

The absence of Hashem's Name from the Megillah reflects that Purim, like Yom Kippur, reaches a level above the Name Havaya, so the Name appears only hidden in initial and final letters, and in 'zeh einenu shoveh li' even backwards.
Just as on Purim one gives to whoever stretches out a hand without checking the order of priority, Hashem on Purim grants every request, even more than on Shabbos.
